thread.title_full: Mayor hopes for buyer for dilapidated property at city council - NewsBreak

author: Mark Caudill
title: Mayor hopes for buyer for dilapidated property at city council - NewsBreak
text:
By Mark Caudill ,
7 hours ago Mansfield Mayor Jodie Perry said there are two ways to look at the ongoing saga over the demolition of the West Park Shopping Center .
One is to fight Namdar Realty, the property owner, in court. She added the company is involved in a number of lawsuits nationally.
But Perry hopes for a more positive result from a buyer with local ties.
"I think at this point, thanks to the generosity of someone local, hopefully we'll have a deal," she said at the Dec. 2 city council meeting. "Between now and Friday (Dec. 5), I'm waiting on an offer to be given from the person to the current owners."
At issue is a Dec. 5 deadline by the Ohio Department of Development regarding the next round of grants for brownfield remediation.
"We have a very tight timeline on this," Perry said.
Council voted Dec. 2 to approve an agreement with the Richland County Land Bank to approve an expenditure of up to $1 million for the demolition of the site and parking lot at 1157 Park Avenue West. Money for the demolition would come from a state grant.
West Park Shopping Center has been an eyesore for years, a far cry from its heyday in the 1950s, when it was the place to shop in this area. West Mansfield Realty, owned by Namdar Realty, bought the property in 2015 for $1.6 million.
Mayor provides update on legal proceedings involving West Park Shopping Center Before the vote, Councilman El Akuchie asked Perry about the status of the legal proceedings.
"If we can rewind back to 2023, it's been going on a lot longer than that, but 2023 was when the demolition orders were put in by the last administration," the mayor said. "There was some back-and-forth because, initially, it was just the building itself (for demolition), and then the city wanted to make sure that the parking lot was also included.
"Quite frankly, they were pushing back on both of them, but they certainly were pushing back on the parking lot. That became the thrust of the back-and-forth."
When Perry took office, the matter was appealed to the city planning commission.
"The law director's office had begun, with outside counsel, working with their counsel," she said. "They were the vinegar, and I was the honey. I have been talking with the owners about how we can get this at the end of the day to a usable site for the community."
Perry said the city would be able to demolish the site and assess it to Namdar's taxes.
"But I'm aware they still owe money on the property, and there's just ways of people getting out of paying bills," she said. "At the end of the day, they would still own the property.
"I've been working with them and then working with people in the community, basically asking if someone who is community-minded could step forward and buy the property. The city would work with the land bank, hoping to get state money for most, if not all, to actually get it torn down."
Perry said the unique aspect of this round of brownfield remediation is that each county has $1 million set aside.
"We expect the demo to be in that range," the mayor said. "If we can't get it together for this round of brownfield development, there will be another round in the future. This is our best shot because of the $1 million set aside."
She said a new prospective owner would likely donate at least a portion of the property to the city for development.
"We'll talk in the future about uses, but we have some ideas," Perry said.
The mayor touched on one more point.
"When a property is on the demo list, the planning commission is supposed to approve the sale," Perry said. "We're not out of line with our ordinance. There's no sale at the moment.
"There is a value in the land itself. The amount will be between the new owner and the old owner, but I think it would be a reasonable amount for the community."
